A bank fee reversal is a customer request decided at the discretion of Chase, not an automatic legal right. Tools for this journey How to Ask Chase to Reverse Outage Fees Asking Chase directly to review and refund charges tied to downtime requires clear documentation and prompt communication. Follow these five steps to submit your request: Identify and list every fee that posted around the November 16 window, noting the exact date, transaction description, and dollar figure. Gather supporting proof, including screenshots of app error messages, connection failure notices from linked tools, and account statements showing attempted payment dates. Contact Chase by phone or in writing through your Chase account. Record the date and time of every conversation, the name or identification number of each representative you speak with, and any reference number assigned to your case. Follow up in writing through your Chase account if you spoke by phone, confirming the details discussed and providing attached copies of your documentation. Submitting this request does not guarantee that Chase will reverse the charge. Each fee reversal remains subject to individual review by Chase. What Chase Said Happened on November 16 According to reporting by NBC News , Chase customers reported trouble logging into accounts and withdrawing funds on Monday, November 16, 2026. Around 4:00 p.m. on X, JPMorganChase said it experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system. Chase confirmed that the problem was not cyber-related. While Chase stated that customers still maintained access to accounts and funds, the bank acknowledged that some transactions were taking longer than normal. The disruption affected online services as well as in-person branch transactions across an institution serving approximately 94 million customer relationships, 5,000 branches, and 15,000 automated teller machines (ATMs). A Chase spokesperson told NBC News around 6:30 p.m. that transactions were posting normally. The report did not state that service was fully restored. Fortune reported that the system problem spread across the Chase website and mobile application to certain branches and third-party financial applications. Plaid noted that its own network operated normally but observed connection problems communicating with Chase accounts, which caused errors when users attempted to link or refresh accounts. A Chase spokesperson told Fortune that technical problems slowed completion times for transactions. Fortune noted that when Chase online banking experienced an outage lasting more than a day in 2010, the bank agreed to refund late fees for customers who missed payment deadlines, provided those customers called Chase to ask. That past decision serves as historical precedent rather than a binding commitment for 2026. What to Document and a Request Script Before speaking to a representative, organize your evidence so you can state the facts clearly. Keep copies of the following items: The dates and exact times you attempted to access your account, transfer funds, or make payments. Account statement lines displaying the posted fees alongside the underlying transactions. Screenshots of mobile application errors, website timeout pages, or third-party transfer alerts. Records showing sufficient funds were present or intended for deposit before the disruption began. A contact log listing the date, time, representative name or ID, and ticket reference number for every interaction. Use this request script as a guide when calling customer service or writing a message through your Chase account: "I am contacting you to request a fee reversal for charges caused by the technical outage on November 16, 2026. As a direct result, my account was assessed a fee on [Date] in the amount of [Dollar Amount]. I attempted to complete this transaction during the downtime, and the delay was outside my control. Please review my account history, waive this charge, and confirm the adjustment in writing." State the facts without asserting that Chase is legally mandated to grant the waiver. Focus on showing that your account remained in good standing prior to the system failure. If you believe an electronic fund transfer was handled incorrectly, federal rules provide a formal procedure. Under 12 CFR 1005.11 , known as Regulation E, an error includes an unauthorized electronic fund transfer, an incorrect electronic fund transfer to or from your account, or the omission of an electronic fund transfer from your periodic statement. The financial institution must investigate if you submit an oral or written notice of error no later than 60 days after the institution sends the periodic statement displaying the disputed item. Your error notice must provide your name and account number, along with the type, date, and dollar amount of the suspected error. Treasury estimates the provision will increase retirement savings by an average of $4.2 billion annually over the 2023 to 2032 period. The statutory framework established by Congress in 26 U.S. Code 414A requires the initial uniform percentage to be not less than 3% and not more than 10% during the employee's first year of participation. After this initial participation period, the plan must automatically increase the employee's contribution rate by 1 percentage point at the start of each subsequent plan year. These annual 1-point increases must continue until the default contribution rate reaches at least 10%, subject to a statutory maximum of 15%. Two distinct federal effective dates apply to these automatic enrollment rules. Under Public Law 117-328 (Division T, Title I, Section 101(c)), the statutory amendments apply to plan years beginning after December 31, 2024. In press release SB-0690, the U.S. Department of the Treasury stated that its final regulations generally apply to plan years beginning after December 31, 2027, giving employers time to make necessary administrative changes. The checked primary sources do not state which date governs a specific workplace plan, and workers should not assume an existing plan is exempt or has until 2028 without reviewing formal plan notices. Employees who are automatically enrolled keep the right to opt out or adjust their contribution amount. Under 26 U.S.C. 414A(b)(3), an employee can elect not to have any salary-reduction contributions made or elect to contribute at a different percentage entirely. When an employee does not select specific investment options for their automatic contributions, the statute requires the plan to invest those amounts in accordance with federal default-investment regulations under 29 CFR 2550.404c-5. Which Plans Are Exempt Several categories of retirement plans are completely exempt from the mandatory automatic enrollment rules under 26 U.S. Code 414A(c) . The federal statute specifically excludes plans established before December 29, 2022, which was the enactment date of Public Law 117-328. This grandfathering provision applies to any cash or deferred arrangement under section 401(k) or annuity contract under section 403(b) in existence prior to that date. The law also exempts distinct employer and plan categories: Small employers that have not normally employed more than 10 employees, remaining exempt until one year after the close of the first taxable year in which the business normally employed more than 10 workers. New businesses that have been in existence, together with any predecessor company, for less than 3 years. Governmental plans. Church plans. SIMPLE 401(k) plans established under section 401(k)(11) of the Internal Revenue Code. The U.S. Department of the Treasury stated that the final regulations clarify these statutory exceptions for qualifying small and new businesses, governmental plans, church plans, and SIMPLE 401(k) plans. If an employer fits into an exempt category, it is not required by federal law to implement automatic enrollment. However, an exempt employer may still choose to offer voluntary automatic enrollment under its own plan terms. Under 26 U.S. Code 414A(b)(3) , every participant has the affirmative right to opt out of contributions entirely or select an alternative contribution percentage that differs from the plan default. You can elect not to have contributions made or elect to contribute at a different percentage. The U.S. Department of the Treasury noted that the final regulations simplify plan communications by allowing certain required notices to be combined. The rules also reduce annual notice requirements for qualifying employees who choose not to participate, provided those workers receive annual reminders and any plan documents they are entitled to request. When you receive an automatic enrollment notice from your employer, examine the details carefully. Check the specified default contribution percentage, the date automatic payroll deductions begin, the annual escalation schedule, and the exact steps required to submit an opt-out election. The Minnesota Department of Revenue (DOR) announced that preliminary property tax levies statewide could increase by a maximum of $949 million over 2026, which is a 6.5% increase. Each local authority's final levy is generally capped at its preliminary levy, but your final tax bill can still be higher or lower than the notice shows because of items excluded by law and changes to your property's valuation or classification. County treasurers mail these notices every November to give property owners time to review proposed spending before city councils, county boards and school boards vote on final levies. Under Minnesota Statutes 275.065 , the notice breaks down what each local taxing authority proposes to collect, lists public meeting dates and provides contact details for public comment. Reviewing the notice line by line shows which local government is driving any tax increase and tells you where to direct your feedback before final levies are certified by December 28, 2026. Tools for this journey home affordability calculator → What Your Truth-in-Taxation Notice Is and What You Can Do A Truth-in-Taxation notice is a parcel-specific estimate of your property taxes for the coming year based on preliminary levies adopted by your local taxing authorities. It is not a bill, and you do not make a payment from it. The county treasurer delivers the notice by first class mail after November 10 and on or before November 24 each year to each taxpayer at the address listed on the county assessment roll, with electronic delivery available upon written request. Under the Minnesota Department of Revenue press release , preliminary levies statewide show property taxes could increase by a maximum of $949 million over 2026, representing a 6.5% overall increase. The Department of Revenue notes that final levies can be set lower, but not higher, than preliminary levies, with limited statutory exceptions. However, your individual parcel's bill could be more or less than the figure shown on the notice. The estimate does not account for certain items excluded by statute, such as special assessments or voter-approved referenda passed after the proposed levies were certified. You can take concrete steps right now: Compare the current-year tax column against the proposed tax column for each local taxing authority. Identify which specific entity, such as your county, city or school district, is proposing the largest dollar or percentage change. Note the meeting dates, times and locations listed on the notice for the authorities responsible for the increase. Attend the public budget meetings between late November and late December to ask questions and comment on proposed spending. Submit written comments directly to the taxing authority using the mailing address, phone number or official website printed on your notice if you cannot attend in person. Final levies must be set by local governments by December 28, 2026. The Department of Revenue then compiles the adopted levies and releases final property tax levy information in February. Why Proposed Taxes Are Rising in 2027 According to the Minnesota Department of Revenue , preliminary figures show property taxes statewide could increase by a maximum of $949 million over 2026, a 6.5% increase. Last year, the final statewide levy increase was $74 million lower than preliminary levies, resulting in a final annual increase of 6.4%. Preliminary levy changes vary significantly depending on the category of taxing authority: Taxing authority type 2026 final levy 2027 preliminary levy Proposed percent change Cities $3.985 billion $4.309 billion 8.1% Counties $4.520 billion $4.887 billion 8.1% Townships $350 million $367 million 4.9% Schools $4.378 billion $4.599 billion 5.0% Special taxing districts $544 million $564 million 3.7% Local budget pressures drive these preliminary numbers. As reported by CBS Minnesota , property taxes could rise by nearly $1 billion statewide, though how much an individual homeowner pays depends on local tax rates and property value. In county-level proposals, Hennepin County pitched an 8.1% levy increase, while Dakota County proposed an 18.5% increase. John McCarthy, chief financial officer of the League of Minnesota Cities, stated that cities are down to "bread-and-butter basic services" and property taxes are "really the only tool that cities have left." Matt Hilgart of the Minnesota Association of Counties cited changes to Medicaid and food assistance under federal law taking effect, which shift costs to counties. The Minnesota Legislature provided one-time property tax relief of $125 million earlier this year. The Department of Revenue also notes that individual Truth-in-Taxation notices do not include the results of November 3, 2026, ballot referenda for operations or capital projects held across 63 school districts. Statewide, 26 of those 63 school referenda passed at least partially. The summarized preliminary data includes these referendum results, but Truth-in-Taxation notices do not include them. How to Read the Notice, Column by Column The layout of your Truth-in-Taxation notice is governed by Minn. Stat. 275.065 subd. 3 . The document displays parcel data alongside an itemized comparison between current-year property taxes and proposed property taxes for each taxing jurisdiction serving your home. Notice element Statutory reference What is displayed on your notice Market value Subd. 3(d) County assessor market value on November 1 for the current tax year and next year; stated as final values. Property classification Subd. 3(d) Classifies the parcel as homestead or nonhomestead residential property. County tax Subd. 3(d) Actual current-year tax paid to the county alongside the proposed county tax amount. City or town tax Subd. 3(d) Actual current-year tax paid to the municipality alongside the proposed municipal tax. State general tax Subd. 3(d) Displays the state general tax; proposed equals final. School district levies Subd. 3(d) Separates voter-approved school operating levies from other local school board levies. Tax credits Subd. 3(d) Displays the agricultural homestead credit or school building bond credit where applicable. Special taxing districts Subd. 3(d) Shows the sum of special taxing districts. Total proposed tax Subd. 3(d) Sum of all taxing authorities showing dollar difference and overall percentage change. Hearing information Subd. 3(c) Meeting dates, times and physical addresses where budgets and levies will be discussed. Authority contact details Subd. 3(c) Official website URLs, telephone contact numbers and mailing addresses for comments. Where tax increment financing or the metropolitan fiscal disparities areawide tax applies to a property, those items are stated separately on the form. If a school referendum was pending at the time the notice was drafted, the notice includes a specific note warning that the final school tax amount may be higher than shown if voters approved the measure. Keep the statutory calendar in mind as you review the notice: November 10 to November 24: County treasurers print and deliver notices by first class mail. November 25 to December 28: Required public budget meetings take place across qualifying local jurisdictions. December 28, 2026: Deadline for local governments to set final 2027 property tax levies. February 2027: The Department of Revenue compiles local certifications and releases final statewide levy data. How to Use the Hearing Public budget meetings give taxpayers a direct forum to review spending decisions before local elected officials take a final binding vote. Under Minn. Stat. 275.065 subd. 3(c) , mandatory public hearings must be held by counties, cities with a population over 500, school districts, regional library authorities and metropolitan taxing districts. According to the Department of Revenue Truth-in-Taxation guidelines , these public meetings must take place between November 25 and December 28, 2026. The statute specifies that meetings must be scheduled after November 24 and must not begin before 6:00 p.m. To find the exact date, time and room location for your city council, county board or school district, check the meeting details printed directly on your parcel notice. At these meetings, the taxing authority discusses its budget and levy, and members of the public must be allowed to speak. If you plan to attend, prepare concise remarks focused on specific budget line items or tax percentage changes shown on your notice. Bring your mailed document to verify the proposed dollar increase for that jurisdiction. If you are unable to attend the scheduled public hearing, use the website, phone number or mailing address printed on the form to submit written comments to elected board members before the final levy certification on December 28. What the Hearing Can and Cannot Change Attending a Truth-in-Taxation meeting allows you to advocate for lower spending before final budgets are locked in, but the meeting has distinct legal limits. Local elected officials can choose to adopt a final levy that is lower than the preliminary levy based on public input. Under Minn. Stat. 275.065 subd. 6(a) , the final levy certified by a city, county, school district, regional library district or metropolitan special taxing district cannot exceed its proposed levy, with limited statutory exceptions: A school district levy where voters approved an operating or capital referendum after the preliminary levy was certified. A city or county levy approved by voters in a referendum after preliminary certification. A levy for principal and interest on voter-approved bonds. State-approved funding needs for natural disaster repairs authorized by the commissioner of revenue. Final tort judgments rendered against the municipality that became final after preliminary levies were set. Changes to statutory levy limits certified after the initial proposed levy deadline. For townships and the state general tax, different rules apply under subdivision 6(b). For a town or the state general tax, the proposed levy equals the final levy, though a township can modify its tax levy if residents authorize a change at a special town meeting held under Minnesota Statutes section 365.52. The public hearing cannot change your property's assessed value or tax classification. Assessor records as of November 1 establish the market value listed on your notice. If you believe your property is incorrectly classified as nonhomestead when it is your primary residence, Minn. Stat. 275.065 subd. 3(g) provides relief: if you deliver satisfactory documentation to the county assessor by the statutory deadline proving the home qualified for homestead status in that assessment year, the assessor must reclassify the property as homestead for taxes payable in 2027. Additionally, under subdivision 3(e), the law mandates that your notice explicitly state that proposed and final taxes do not include special assessments, natural disaster cleanup costs, final tort judgments, contamination taxes or voter-approved referenda passed after certified proposals. Because these exclusions exist, never treat the total proposed figure as a ceiling on your final tax bill. Your ultimate property tax bill could be more or less than the notice indicates. Our Takeaway For Minnesota homeowners with a proposed-tax notice, remember that this document is a preliminary estimate rather than a bill. Each taxing authority's final levy is generally capped at its proposed levy according to the Minnesota Department of Revenue, but your final bill can still differ because of statutory exclusions under subdivision 3(e), such as special assessments and post-certification referenda, as well as separate valuation and classification determinations. Compare the current and proposed numbers for each taxing district, identify which entity is driving the change and attend that authority's public hearing before final votes are cast. Use the home affordability calculator to test how a tax change shifts your monthly payment, and read homeowner tax deductions for what you can write off. Then attend your local budget hearing before December 28 to give your input on spending. Frequently asked questions Is a Truth-in-Taxation notice a bill? No, a Truth-in-Taxation notice is not a bill, and you do not pay the amount listed. It is a parcel-specific proposal showing what your property taxes would be if local taxing authorities adopt their preliminary budgets. Can my property tax go up after the notice? Yes, your final tax bill could be more or less than the proposed amount. While local authorities generally cannot raise their final levies above preliminary numbers, final tax bills can rise due to items excluded from the notice, including special assessments, later voter-approved referenda, disaster cleanup levies and final tort judgments. When are final levies set? According to the Minnesota Department of Revenue, local governments must set final 2027 property tax levies by December 28, 2026. The Minnesota Department of Revenue compiles those local certifications and publishes final property tax levy information in February 2027. Which governments must hold a hearing? Counties, school districts, regional library authorities, metropolitan taxing districts and cities with populations over 500 must hold a public hearing between November 25 and December 28, 2026. What does the notice leave out? Under Minnesota law, the notice excludes special assessments, voter-approved referenda passed after proposed taxes are certified, post-certification disaster cleanup costs, post-certification tort judgments and contamination taxes on remediated property. What if my notice lists my home as nonhomestead? If your primary residence is listed as nonhomestead, contact your county assessor immediately. Under Minnesota Statutes 275.065 subdivision 3(g), providing satisfactory documentation to the county assessor by the applicable deadline requires the assessor to reclassify qualifying property as homestead for the upcoming tax year. How Much Emergency Fund Do I Need? By Jonathan Velez , Personal Finance Writer & Editor · Reviewed against primary sources · Updated June 25, 2026 You need an emergency fund equal to 3 to 6 months of your essential monthly expenses, not your total income. Basing the fund on your needs alone, rather than your full paycheck, often cuts the target in half. This guide shows you how to set that number, when to hold more or less, where to keep the cash, and how to build the fund. Tools for this journey Monthly budget → 50/30/20 budget → Savings goal → Size it on essential expenses, not income Your emergency fund should cover essential monthly expenses, not your whole income. Essentials are the bills you cannot skip: rent or mortgage, utilities, groceries, insurance, transportation, and minimum debt payments. Leave out the extras. Dining out, travel, subscriptions, and shopping are wants, not needs. In a real emergency, you pause those costs, so your fund does not have to replace them. This is the point most people miss. Sizing a fund on gross income can nearly double the target for no reason. Add up your true essentials first -- our budget tools make that quick -- then multiply by the number of months you want to cover. A worked example: $3,000 a month Say your essential expenses come to $3,000 a month. Three months of coverage is $9,000. Six months is $18,000. That range, $9,000 to $18,000, is your target. Pick a point in the range based on your risk. A stable two-income household might aim near $9,000. A single earner with variable pay leans toward $18,000. Use our savings goal calculator to turn that target into a monthly savings plan you can actually follow. When to hold more than the minimum Hold closer to 6 months -- or more -- when your income is less certain or harder to replace. Several situations call for a bigger cushion. **One income.** A single earner has no second paycheck as backup. **Sole earner for a family.** More people depend on that one income. **Variable or self-employed income.** Freelancers and commission earners face uneven months, so 6 to 12 months is safer. **A shaky job or industry.** If layoffs are a real risk, a longer runway buys time. **A long expected job search.** Senior or specialized roles can take many months to replace. The less predictable your income, the more months you want saved. When 3 months is enough Three months of essential expenses can be enough when your income is stable and backed up. Two steady salaries in one household are the clearest case. If one partner loses a job, the other paycheck still covers part of the bills. That shared safety net lowers how much cash you must hold. Other signs you can sit at the lower end: strong job security, an in-demand skill, and no dependents relying only on you. You can always build past 3 months later, but reaching that first milestone matters most. Where to keep your emergency fund Keep your emergency fund in a high-yield savings account that is FDIC-insured and easy to reach. The money must be safe and available the day you need it. The FDIC automatically insures deposits up to at least $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank. A savings account keeps your cash protected while it earns interest. Skip investments like stocks for this money. Their value can drop right when an emergency hits. Also skip a plain checking account, where idle cash earns almost nothing and is easy to spend by accident. One caution: do not treat a credit card as your emergency fund. If you already carry a balance, see how long it takes to pay off a credit card to understand the real cost. If a bank outage causes late or overdraft fees, read what to do about bank fees after an outage for how to ask for a reversal. Build it in the right order Build your emergency fund in two stages so early progress feels reachable. First, save a small starter fund of $1,000 to $2,000. This covers most surprise bills, like a car repair or a medical copay. A starter fund also keeps a small emergency from turning into high-interest debt. Once it is in place, grow the fund toward your full 3-to-6-month target. Wondering whether to finish the fund before investing or clearing debt? See our guide on whether to pay off debt or invest to sequence the rest of your plan. Two quick self-checks beyond the dollar target A 3-to-6-month fund is the target, but two quick questions show whether you are actually secure today, not just on paper. First: could you cover a $1,000 surprise bill without touching a credit card? If the honest answer is no, you are relying on credit as a backstop, not savings. That gap matters even if your fund technically meets the 3-month minimum, since a card balance carries interest your savings never will. Second: how many weeks of essential bills could you cover the day your income stopped? Add up your checking and savings balances, then divide by your weekly essential spend from the first section above. If the number is under four weeks, treat building the starter fund as your most urgent money goal, ahead of extra debt payments or new investing. Frequently asked questions How much emergency fund do I need? You need 3 to 6 months of your essential monthly expenses, not 3 to 6 months of income. Add up rent, utilities, groceries, insurance, transportation, and minimum debt payments. Then multiply by 3 for the low end and 6 for the high end. Should an emergency fund be based on income or expenses? Expenses -- specifically your essential expenses. In an emergency you cut wants like dining out and travel, so your fund only needs to cover needs. Sizing it on your full income can nearly double the target for no reason. How much should I save before I start investing? Save a starter fund of $1,000 to $2,000 first, then build toward 3 to 6 months of essential expenses. A starter fund keeps a small emergency from becoming credit card debt before you invest or attack other debt. Where should I keep my emergency fund? In a high-yield savings account that is FDIC-insured and liquid. FDIC insurance protects deposits up to at least $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank. A savings account also lets the cash earn interest while staying easy to reach. Avoid stocks, which can fall right when you need the money. How many months should I save if I am self-employed? Aim for 6 to 12 months of essential expenses if your income is variable or self-employed. Uneven months and slow seasons make a longer cushion safer than the standard 3 to 6 months. A single earner supporting a family should also lean toward the higher end. Why do I need an emergency fund? An emergency fund keeps a surprise cost from turning into high-interest debt. The Federal Reserve found that in 2024, only 63% of adults could cover a $400 emergency with cash or its equivalent. A dedicated fund means a car repair or medical bill does not derail your budget. How do I know if I'm secretly relying on credit instead of savings? Ask whether you could cover a $1,000 surprise bill without touching a credit card. If not, your card is functioning as your real emergency fund, and it charges interest yours never will. Building even a $1,000 starter fund removes that gap. How much emergency fund is too much? An emergency fund is too large once the balance sits well past your range, typically 6 months of essential expenses for most households or 6 to 12 for variable income. To check your numbers, add up your current monthly essential expenses, multiply by your target months, and compare that figure with your balance. Any cash above that personal target can go toward other financial goals. To sequence your next steps, see our guide on whether to pay off debt or invest . How much emergency fund should a couple or a family have? There is no separate target by household size, so couples and families still aim for 3 to 6 months of essential monthly expenses rather than income. Stable two-income households can aim near 3 months because the other paycheck still covers part of the bills, while a family's sole earner should lean toward 6 months or more. To calculate your dollar goal, add up household essentials for rent or mortgage, utilities, groceries, insurance, transportation, and minimum debt payments, then multiply by your months. For example, if your household's essentials total $3,000 a month, 3 months is $9,000 and 6 months is $18,000. You can total your household essentials using our monthly budget calculator . itemListElement.name: How Much Emergency Fund Do I Need?

mainEntity.name: How much emergency fund do I need?

acceptedAnswer.text: You need 3 to 6 months of your essential monthly expenses, not 3 to 6 months of income. Add up rent, utilities, groceries, insurance, transportation, and minimum debt payments. Then multiply by 3 for the low end and 6 for the high end.

mainEntity.name: Should an emergency fund be based on income or expenses?

acceptedAnswer.text: Expenses -- specifically your essential expenses. In an emergency you cut wants like dining out and travel, so your fund only needs to cover needs. Sizing it on your full income can nearly double the target for no reason.

mainEntity.name: How much should I save before I start investing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Save a starter fund of $1,000 to $2,000 first, then build toward 3 to 6 months of essential expenses. A starter fund keeps a small emergency from becoming credit card debt before you invest or attack other debt.

mainEntity.name: Where should I keep my emergency fund?

acceptedAnswer.text: In a high-yield savings account that is FDIC-insured and liquid. FDIC insurance protects deposits up to at least $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank. A savings account also lets the cash earn interest while staying easy to reach. Avoid stocks, which can fall right when you need the money.

mainEntity.name: How many months should I save if I am self-employed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Aim for 6 to 12 months of essential expenses if your income is variable or self-employed. Uneven months and slow seasons make a longer cushion safer than the standard 3 to 6 months. A single earner supporting a family should also lean toward the higher end.

mainEntity.name: Why do I need an emergency fund?

acceptedAnswer.text: An emergency fund keeps a surprise cost from turning into high-interest debt. The Federal Reserve found that in 2024, only 63% of adults could cover a $400 emergency with cash or its equivalent. A dedicated fund means a car repair or medical bill does not derail your budget.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if I'm secretly relying on credit instead of savings?

acceptedAnswer.text: Ask whether you could cover a $1,000 surprise bill without touching a credit card. If not, your card is functioning as your real emergency fund, and it charges interest yours never will. Building even a $1,000 starter fund removes that gap.

mainEntity.name: How much emergency fund is too much?

acceptedAnswer.text: An emergency fund is too large once the balance sits well past your range, typically 6 months of essential expenses for most households or 6 to 12 for variable income. To check your numbers, add up your current monthly essential expenses, multiply by your target months, and compare that figure with your balance. Any cash above that personal target can go toward other financial goals. To sequence your next steps, see our guide on whether to pay off debt or invest.

mainEntity.name: How much emergency fund should a couple or a family have?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no separate target by household size, so couples and families still aim for 3 to 6 months of essential monthly expenses rather than income. Stable two-income households can aim near 3 months because the other paycheck still covers part of the bills, while a family's sole earner should lean toward 6 months or more. To calculate your dollar goal, add up household essentials for rent or mortgage, utilities, groceries, insurance, transportation, and minimum debt payments, then multiply by your months. For example, if your household's essentials total $3,000 a month, 3 months is $9,000 and 6 months is $18,000. You can total your household essentials using our monthly budget calculator.

The mistake we see readers make most often is treating Roth and Traditional contributions as if they have separate limits. The IRS (Internal Revenue Service) treats them as one shared number. Workers 50 and older get a catch-up contribution on top of that cap, while workers ages 60 to 63 get a bigger one under the SECURE 2.0 Act . Tools for this journey 401(k) calculator → Retirement → Roth IRA calculator → The 401(k) Contribution Limit for 2026 The 2026 401(k) employee contribution limit is $24,500, according to the IRS. That number covers your own paycheck deferrals only, whether you route them to a Traditional 401(k), a Roth 401(k), or split between the two. Contributions have to reach your plan through payroll by December 31. An IRA (Individual Retirement Account) gives you until the following April's tax deadline to fund the prior year, but a 401(k) does not. Miss the calendar year and that year's room is gone. The limit moves almost every year with inflation. It rose from $23,000 in 2024 to $23,500 in 2025 to $24,500 in 2026, a bigger jump than most years because inflation ran higher. Check the IRS's own contribution-limit page before you set next year's payroll deferral, rather than relying on a number from an old article. If you are setting 2027 elections, the 2027 401(k) and IRA limits guide covers the new deferral limit and catch-up amounts. For plans that enroll workers automatically, see the automatic enrollment rules for new plans . The Roth and Traditional Caps Share One Number Your Roth 401(k) and Traditional 401(k) contributions draw from the same $24,500 limit, not two separate ones. Put $15,000 into the Traditional side and you have $9,500 of room left for Roth, no more. People often ask whether the Roth and Traditional caps combine, or whether each side gets its own number. They combine. The IRS treats a Traditional 401(k) dollar and a Roth 401(k) dollar as the same kind of contribution against the cap, even though the two get opposite tax treatment later. Your employer's match is the one piece that stays outside this number. A match always lands in the Traditional side of your account, pre-tax, no matter which option you picked for your own deferrals. Choose 100% Roth for your own contributions and you still end up with a Traditional balance from the match, taxed on withdrawal. See Roth 401(k) vs Traditional 401(k) for the tax math behind which side wins for your bracket. How Much to Split Between Roth and Traditional A common approach is splitting close to 50/50 between Roth and Traditional, so neither a higher nor a lower future tax rate wrecks the whole plan. Take a worker earning $70,000 who contributes 10% of pay, or $7,000, to their 401(k). Putting half in each side means $3,500 grows tax-free in the Roth and $3,500 lowers this year's taxable income in the Traditional account. A 50/50 split is not for someone certain their tax rate will fall sharply in retirement, such as a high earner nearing a planned early retirement with a much smaller expected income. That person usually comes out ahead putting closer to 100% in the Traditional side now and converting to Roth later, when the lower bracket makes the conversion cheap. The split should move when a new fact changes the tax-rate bet behind it. A big pay raise that pushes this year's rate higher is one trigger. A pension or Social Security stream large enough to keep retirement income high is another, and so is new tax legislation that changes future brackets. Run your own numbers through the 401(k) calculator whenever one of those changes. Catch-Up Contributions for Age 50 and Up Workers 50 and older can add an $8,000 catch-up contribution on top of the $24,500 base limit for 2026, for a total of $32,500. That catch-up applies whether the extra money goes to the Roth side, the Traditional side, or both. Workers 60 to 63 get a bigger number instead of the standard catch-up. Under the SECURE 2.0 Act, that group can contribute an $11,250 catch-up, bringing their total to $35,750 for the year. The higher catch-up applies only in the calendar year you turn 60 through the year you turn 63. Turn 64, and the catch-up drops back to the standard $8,000. A worker who turns 60 in 2026 and maxes out the full $35,750 gets $11,250 more into the account than someone under 50 contributing the base $24,500 alone. That extra money only has a handful of years left to compound before retirement typically starts. Run the gap through the 401(k) calculator to see what it adds to your own payout. The $72,000 Combined Employer and Employee Limit Your own paycheck deferrals and everything your employer adds are capped together at $72,000 for 2026, a separate and much higher number than the $24,500 you control directly. This combined limit covers your deferrals, any employer match, and any profit-sharing contribution the plan makes on top. Reaching $72,000 usually takes a generous employer contribution, since $24,500 from your own paycheck alone leaves $47,500 of room. A business owner running a Solo 401(k) is the case most likely to bump into this ceiling. The same person acts as both the employee and the employer making the profit-sharing contribution, so both halves of the $72,000 cap come from one paycheck. An employee at a typical company with a 4% or 5% match rarely gets close. The catch-up contribution sits outside the $72,000 combined limit. A worker 50 or older can still add the full $8,000 (or $11,250 at 60 to 63) even after combined employee-and-employer contributions hit the $72,000 mark. By Jonathan Velez , Personal Finance Writer & Editor · Reviewed against primary sources · Updated October 17, 2026 With a Roth 401(k), you contribute after-tax dollars and make tax-free withdrawals in retirement. A Traditional 401(k), by contrast, reduces your taxable income today. The right choice depends on whether your tax rate is higher now or in retirement. Roth 401(k) vs Traditional 401(k): Side-by-Side Roth 401(k) Traditional 401(k) Contribution tax timing After-tax (no deduction now) Pre-tax (reduces taxable income now) 2026 contribution limit $24,500 ($32,500 if 50+) $24,500 ($32,500 if 50+) Tax on retirement withdrawals Tax-free Taxed as ordinary income Employer match taxation Pre-tax by default; a plan may let you take vested match as Roth Pre-tax Required minimum distributions None during the owner's lifetime (beneficiaries still follow RMD rules) Yes, generally starting at age 73 Income limits None None Best for Early career, expect higher taxes in retirement Peak earning years, expect lower taxes in retirement 📣 Building in finance? Put your product in front of readers comparing options on this page. Advertise With Us → Which should you choose? Pick Roth 401(k) if you're early in your career or expect your tax rate to be higher in retirement (very common given potential Social Security income and tax law uncertainty). Pick Traditional 401(k) in your peak earning years when today's tax rate is likely your highest, and you're confident you'll be in a lower bracket in retirement. Tax math: which version saves more? The decision is a tax-rate bet. If your rate is 22% today and 12% in retirement, every Traditional 401(k) dollar saves 22 cents in tax now and costs only 12 cents when withdrawn — a 10-cent savings per dollar. Roth 401(k) would have been the wrong choice in that scenario. Flip it: if you're 28, earning $55,000, and in the 12% bracket today — but expect a 22% rate in retirement with Social Security, pension income, and required withdrawals from pre-tax accounts — the Roth 401(k) saves 10 cents per dollar. The honest answer is nobody knows for certain what future tax rates will be. That's why many financial planners recommend diversifying: split contributions between Roth and Traditional to hedge the uncertainty. The employer match goes in pre-tax by default Employer matching contributions go into the pre-tax (Traditional) side of a 401(k) by default, even if all of your own deferrals go to the Roth 401(k) option. A 100% Roth 401(k) saver can therefore build a Traditional balance from the match. Plan for that mixed tax treatment. Since the SECURE 2.0 Act (2022), a plan may let you take your match as Roth. Section 604 makes this optional, so employers are not required to offer it. Only vested match money qualifies, and a Roth match is not excludable from your gross income. To see whether your plan offers a Roth match, check the plan document or ask HR. The IRS sets out the rule in Notice 2024-2, Part L . Roth 401(k) and required minimum distributions Roth 401(k) balances have no required minimum distributions (RMDs) while the owner is alive. The IRS RMD FAQ states that RMD rules do not apply to Roth IRAs or designated Roth accounts, such as a Roth 401(k), during the owner's lifetime. Traditional 401(k) balances follow different rules. RMDs on those generally begin at age 73. In a plan that holds both kinds of money, RMDs apply to the traditional balance and not to the Roth balance. Beneficiaries are a separate case. Anyone who inherits a Roth 401(k) or a Roth IRA is still subject to RMD rules. Rolling a Roth 401(k) into a Roth IRA is optional and is not required to avoid lifetime RMDs. For the full side-by-side, see Roth IRA vs Roth 401(k) . When to use both at the same time If your plan allows split contributions, you can put some dollars in Traditional and some in Roth each year. In 2026, as long as the total doesn't exceed $24,500, you can split it any way you like. A practical approach: contribute enough Traditional 401(k) to stay in your current bracket's lower band, then put additional contributions in Roth. For example, if you're $5,000 below the top of the 22% bracket, put $5,000 Traditional (saving at 22%) and the rest Roth. Use the retirement calculator to model both approaches with your specific income and expected retirement spending, or test your own tax rates in the Roth vs Traditional 401(k) calculator . If your employer enrolls you automatically, read how 401(k) automatic enrollment defaults work for the starting rate and your opt-out right. For more detail, see 401k Calculator . Frequently asked questions Should I choose Roth or Traditional 401(k)? Choose Roth 401(k) if you're early in your career and expect a higher tax rate in retirement. Choose Traditional 401(k) in your peak earning years when your current rate is high. Many financial planners recommend splitting contributions to hedge tax uncertainty. For more detail, see 401(k) vs Roth IRA . Can I have both a Roth and Traditional 401(k) in the same plan? Yes, if your employer's plan allows it. You can split your contributions between Roth and Traditional in any proportion, as long as the combined total doesn't exceed the annual limit ($24,500 in 2026). For more detail, see 401(k) Contribution Limits for 2026 . Do Roth 401(k) contributions reduce my taxable income? No. Roth 401(k) contributions are made with after-tax money, so they don't reduce your current year's taxable income. Traditional 401(k) contributions do reduce your taxable income. Is the Roth 401(k) better than a Roth IRA? The Roth 401(k) has no income limits and a much higher contribution limit ($24,500 vs $7,500 in 2026). The Roth IRA often has more investment options. Most people should use both: max the Roth IRA, then use the Roth 401(k) for additional savings. When can I withdraw Roth 401(k) money tax-free? Roth 401(k) money comes out fully tax-free only as a qualified distribution, which generally means a 5-year participation period has passed and the withdrawal happens on or after age 59½, after death, or due to disability. The 5-year period starts on the first day of the taxable year of your first designated Roth contribution and ends after five consecutive taxable years. In a nonqualified withdrawal, only the contribution share is tax-free: in the IRS example , $5,000 taken from an account holding $9,400 of contributions and $600 of earnings splits into $4,700 tax-free and $300 of taxable earnings. Many buyers assume that buying a home immediately lowers their tax bill. For a married couple filing jointly in 2026, the standard deduction is $32,200, which means an average mortgage balance often generates less write-off value than taking the standard amount. Determining whether you come out ahead requires running the actual numbers on your interest, real estate taxes, and other qualified expenses before choosing Schedule A. Tools for this journey Mortgage calculator hub → Closing cost calculator → Home affordability → HELOC calculator → Do Your Deductions Beat the Standard Deduction A homeowner only benefits from deducting housing costs if their combined itemized expenses exceed the standard deduction for their tax filing status. Under the IRS inflation adjustments for tax year 2026 , the standard deduction is $16,100 for single filers and married individuals filing separately, $24,150 for heads of household, and $32,200 for married couples filing jointly. Unless your total itemized deductions surpass those thresholds, you claim the standard deduction instead. Consider a hypothetical worked example of a $400,000 30-year fixed mortgage at an interest rate of 6.5%. The monthly principal-and-interest payment is $2,528.27, generating roughly $25,868.36 of interest in the first full year. If that household pays $5,000 in annual property taxes, their baseline housing deductions total $30,868. For a married couple filing jointly, that $30,868 total sits below the $32,200 standard deduction, so itemizing purely on those two items yields no tax advantage. That couple would need at least $1,332 in additional itemized deductions, such as charitable gifts or state income taxes, before itemizing provides a financial gain. With smaller balances, the gap widens. A $300,000 mortgage at 6.5% has a monthly payment of $1,896.20 and generates about $19,401.27 of interest during the first year. Even with $5,000 in property taxes, the total deduction reaches $24,401.27, leaving a married couple thousands of dollars short of the $32,200 threshold. You can estimate your own amortization schedule using our mortgage calculator hub to check your specific first-year interest amount. Mortgage Interest Deductions and Debt Limits Homeowners who itemize can deduct the interest paid on debt used to acquire or substantially improve their primary or secondary residence. According to IRS Publication 936 and IRS Topic 505 , mortgage interest is deductible on acquisition debt up to $750,000 for single filers and married couples filing jointly, or $375,000 for married filers filing separately, on homes acquired after December 15, 2017. A higher grandfathered limit of $1 million, or $500,000 for married filing separately, applies to mortgages originated on or before December 15, 2017. Each January, your mortgage servicer reports the exact interest you paid during the prior calendar year on Form 1098. If your total qualifying mortgage balance across all properties exceeds the $750,000 acquisition debt limit, you cannot deduct the interest attributable to the excess balance. Review our guide on mortgage early payoff tax implications to evaluate how accelerating payments impacts your annual interest deduction. Home Equity Loan and Line of Credit Interest Interest on a home equity loan or a home equity line of credit is deductible only when the borrowed funds are spent to buy, build, or substantially improve the home that secures the loan. Per IRS Publication 936 , 'No matter when the indebtedness was incurred, you can no longer deduct the interest from a loan secured by your home to the extent the loan proceeds weren't used to buy, build, or substantially improve your home.' Any debt secured by your home also counts against the overall $750,000 acquisition indebtedness ceiling. The specific use of the loan proceeds dictates its tax deductibility. If you take out a $50,000 home equity loan to remodel your kitchen, replace a roof, or construct an addition, the interest qualifies for deduction. Conversely, if you tap home equity to consolidate personal credit card debt, finance a car purchase, or pay college tuition, none of that interest can be deducted. Explore our breakdown of HELOC vs home equity loan options and run figures through our HELOC calculator to see the monthly payment impact. Deducting Mortgage Discount Points Discount points paid upfront to lower your mortgage interest rate can be deducted on Schedule A, either immediately in the year paid or spread across the loan term. As outlined in IRS Topic 505 and IRS Publication 936 , points paid on a purchase mortgage for your primary residence can generally be deducted in full in the year you pay them if specific requirements are met. The loan must be used to purchase or build your main home, and the points must be clearly shown as points on your settlement statement. When points do not qualify for immediate full deduction, they must be deducted ratably over the life of the mortgage. Points paid by a seller cannot be deducted by the buyer as interest. To calculate upfront financing expenses on a prospective purchase, check our closing cost calculator . Property Taxes and the State and Local Tax Cap Real estate property taxes assessed by state or local governments are deductible as an itemized expense on Schedule A within statutory limits. Under IRS Topic 503 , state and local real property taxes are combined with other state and local taxes, including income or sales taxes, subject to an aggregate state and local tax deduction cap. The state and local tax deduction cap is set at $40,000 for 2025, or $20,000 for married individuals filing separately, and the cap cannot be reduced below $10,000. Under current law, this cap is scheduled to rise 1% annually, making the cap $40,400 for 2026, though filers should verify the current figure directly at IRS Topic 503 . Check the amount on your county property tax statement, because only taxes actually paid count. If you own in Minnesota, see how to read a Minnesota proposed property tax notice for what the November notice means for next year's bill. Home Office Deductions for Eligible Homeowners Homeowners who run an independent business or work as self-employed individuals may deduct qualifying home office expenses, but regular corporate employees cannot. Under rules from the IRS simplified home office option , qualified taxpayers can claim a simplified deduction of $5 per square foot for a dedicated work area, up to a maximum of 300 square feet, which produces a top deduction of $1,500. Alternatively, filers can calculate actual expenses based on the square footage percentage of housing costs, including utilities, insurance, and depreciation. To qualify under either method, the home office space must be used exclusively and on a regular basis as your principal place of business or to meet clients. Employees receiving a Form W-2 cannot claim a home office deduction under current federal rules, because miscellaneous itemized deductions for unreimbursed employee business expenses were eliminated for tax years beginning after 2017. Medically Necessary Home Improvements Capital improvements made to your home for medical care qualify as itemized medical deductions only to the extent the expense exceeds any increase in property value. According to IRS Publication 502 and IRS Topic 502 , capital expenditures made primarily for medical care, such as widening doorways, installing wheelchair ramps, lowering kitchen counters, or adding a chairlift, count toward your medical expense calculation. However, if an improvement increases the market value of your residence, the deductible amount is strictly limited to the difference between the actual construction cost and the corresponding increase in the home's appraisal value. Total qualified medical expenses are only deductible on Schedule A to the extent they exceed 7.5% of your adjusted gross income, commonly abbreviated as AGI. For example, if your adjusted gross income is $100,000, only medical expenses exceeding $7,500 can be factored into your itemized deductions. Homeowner Expenses That Are Not Deductible Many recurring expenses associated with owning real estate do not qualify for federal tax deductions on a primary personal residence. IRS guidance specifies that regular personal housing outlays are not deductible on Schedule A: Mortgage principal payments Homeowners insurance and hazard insurance premiums Routine maintenance costs and general repairs Utilities including electricity, natural gas, trash, and water Homeowners association fees, commonly known as HOA dues Unlike capital improvements that get added to your property basis, routine repairs such as fixing a roof leak or repainting a wall do not lower your current taxable income. In addition, the itemized deduction for private mortgage insurance premiums is noted in IRS Publication 936 as expired, and tax law changes in 2025 affect this area, so consult the current version of the publication to confirm whether any recent legislation reinstates the deduction for your filing year. Filing Preparation and Recordkeeping Steps Organizing real estate documentation before tax season ensures you do not miss qualifying deductions or claim invalid write-offs. Follow these practical steps when preparing your annual filing: Gather your Form 1098 statements from all mortgage servicers that held your loan during the calendar year. Review your closing disclosure if you purchased or refinanced during the tax year to verify whether discount points were itemized. Check your county property tax statements to verify the exact tax payments disbursed within the tax year. Keep paid receipts and contractor invoices for any medical modifications or substantial improvements funded via home equity. Verify the current treatment of mortgage insurance premiums in IRS Publication 936 to check if your policy qualifies under newly enacted rules. Comparing these gathered records against the standard deduction threshold helps you decide whether filing Schedule A is worth the effort. For a broad inventory of deductions outside real estate, consult our tax deductions checklist . Who This Deductibility Math Does Not Serve The standard deduction test produces very different outcomes depending on debt balance and location. Itemizing real estate deductions does not benefit homeowners with small mortgage balances or paid-off homes, especially married filers in low-property-tax states. If you are married filing jointly and your total annual mortgage interest and local taxes stay well below $32,200, tracking individual receipts provides zero tax reduction compared to taking the standard allowance. First-time buyers can evaluate baseline costs using our first time home buyer guide or test borrowing limits on the home affordability calculator . Our verdict would flip if a buyer holds a substantial mortgage balance, such as a $700,000 loan at a high interest rate, paired with higher property taxes and charitable donations that push itemized deductions comfortably above the standard deduction threshold. Calculate your total deductible expenses each filing season, because annual principal amortization lowers your deductible interest each year, eventually making the standard deduction the superior choice. Frequently asked questions Is mortgage interest tax deductible in 2026? Yes, mortgage interest is deductible on acquisition debt up to $750,000 for single and joint filers, or $375,000 for married individuals filing separately, for homes acquired after December 15, 2017. You must itemize deductions on Schedule A to claim it, and loans originating before December 16, 2017, qualify under an older $1 million limit. Are property taxes deductible? Yes, state and local property taxes are deductible on Schedule A, subject to the combined state and local tax deduction cap. For 2025, that cap is $40,000, or $20,000 for married filers filing separately, with a statutory floor of $10,000 and an annual 1% increase that makes the cap $40,400 for 2026. Can I deduct home equity loan or HELOC interest? You can deduct interest on a home equity loan or line of credit only if the borrowed money was used to buy, build, or substantially improve the home securing the loan. If the funds were used for other purposes, such as paying down personal loans or funding college tuition, the interest is not deductible. Can I deduct home improvements? Standard home renovations and routine repairs are not deductible, but medically necessary modifications may qualify under Schedule A medical expense deductions. The deductible amount is restricted to the cost that exceeds any increase in the market value of your property, and total medical expenses must surpass 7.5% of your adjusted gross income. Should I itemize or take the standard deduction as a homeowner? You should itemize only if your total qualifying deductions, including mortgage interest, property taxes, points, and other allowable write-offs, exceed the standard deduction for your filing status. For 2026, the standard deduction is $16,100 for single filers, $24,150 for heads of household, and $32,200 for married couples filing jointly.
